name: Russian Checkers
intro: Learn Russian Checkers (shashki) from scratch: moving, capturing backwards, flying kings, crowning mid-capture and the Turkish strike, then the combinations and endgames that win games.

ladder.name: Penny
ladder.blurb: Just learned the moves. Walks into captures.

ladder.name: Mira
ladder.blurb: Steady player. Spots the simple combinations.

ladder.name: The Monocle
ladder.blurb: Reads long captures ahead. Loves a flying king.

units.name: How Russian Checkers works
units.blurb: The board, moving, capturing both ways, flying kings and how you win.

lessons.title: The Russian Checkers board and how to set it up
lessons.summary: How to set up a Russian Checkers (shashki) board: 12 men each on the dark squares, a dark corner on your left, and the main road.
lessons.wrap: That’s the starting position. Next: how the men move.

steps.text:
Russian Checkers, or shashki, uses the same board as ordinary checkers: 8×8, with play only on the dark squares. Each player has 12 men on the dark squares of the three rows nearest them.

The two middle rows start empty.

Each player has a dark square in the bottom-left corner (a1 for you).

The long diagonal from a1 to h8 is called the main road. It’s the most important line on the board, as you’ll see when kings appear.
Quick check.
steps.prompt: In Russian Checkers, which side moves first?
steps.explain: White moves first in Russian Checkers. On BoardGameSite you play gold, which takes White’s role and moves first.

lessons.title: How the men move in Russian Checkers
lessons.summary: A man in Russian Checkers steps one square diagonally forward onto an empty dark square. Practise moving on a real board.
lessons.wrap: One step, diagonally, forwards. Next: capturing, where Russian rules start to differ.

steps.text:
An ordinary piece is called a man. A man moves one square diagonally forward onto an empty dark square.

A man never steps backwards or sideways. (Capturing is different, as you’ll see next.)
Your man on d4 has two choices.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this man can move to.
steps.done: c5 and e5: the two forward diagonals.

steps.text: Your turn. Tap your man, then the square to move it to.
steps.prompt: Move your man forward.
steps.done: That’s a move. Then it’s your opponent’s turn.

lessons.title: Capturing backwards in Russian Checkers
lessons.summary: In Russian Checkers a man captures by jumping an enemy piece, forwards or backwards, and captures are compulsory. Learn with puzzles.
lessons.wrap: Men capture in all four directions, and a capture must be taken. Next: capturing several pieces in one move.

steps.text: If an enemy piece is diagonally next to yours and the square straight beyond it is empty, you capture it by jumping over it. The captured piece comes off the board.
Your man on d4 can jump the black man on e5.
steps.prompt: Capture the black man.
steps.done: Captured. Your man lands on f6.

steps.text:
Here is the big difference from American checkers: in Russian Checkers a man can also capture backwards.

Men only step forwards, but they capture in all four diagonal directions.
The black man on d4 has slipped behind your man.
steps.prompt: Capture it by jumping backwards.
steps.done: A backward capture. In Russian Checkers no piece is safe just because it’s behind you.

steps.text: One more rule.
steps.prompt: You can capture, but you’d rather make a different move. Can you?
steps.explain: No. If any capture is available, you must take one.

lessons.title: Multiple captures in Russian Checkers
lessons.summary: After a capture, if your piece can capture again it must keep going, even backwards. Learn multiple captures in Russian Checkers.
lessons.wrap: Once you start capturing, you finish the chain. Next: flying kings.

steps.text: If, after a capture, your piece can capture again, it must keep going in the same move. The chain can change direction, and it can turn backwards.
Tap your man, then each landing square in turn.
steps.prompt: Capture both black men in one move.
steps.wrong: Jump to c5 first, then keep going: the man on d4 can be taken backwards.
steps.done: Two in one move, the second one backwards.

steps.text: Your man on e3 can take one piece (d4) or two (f4, then f6).
steps.prompt: Which captures are allowed in Russian Checkers?
options: Only the one that takes the most pieces
steps.explain: You choose. Captures are compulsory, but you don’t have to take the biggest one. (International draughts is different: there you must take the most.) Once you pick a capture, though, you must finish it.

lessons.title: Flying kings in Russian Checkers
lessons.summary: A Russian Checkers king flies any distance along a diagonal and captures from afar. Learn how kings move and capture, with puzzles.
lessons.wrap: A flying king is worth about three men. Next: crowning in the middle of a capture.

steps.text: A man that reaches the far row becomes a king (damka). Russian kings fly: they move any number of empty squares along a diagonal, forwards or backwards, like a bishop in chess.
Your king is on d4.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this king can move to.
steps.wrong: Any distance along any diagonal, until something is in the way.
steps.done: Twelve squares! The man on h8 blocks the last one.

steps.text: A king captures from a distance too: the squares up to the enemy piece must be empty, and it can land on any empty square beyond.
steps.prompt: Capture the man on e5.
steps.done: Captured from three squares away.

steps.text:
If one of the landing squares lets the king capture again, it must land there and carry on.

Here, after jumping c3, only e5 lets the king go on to take f4.
Tap your king, then each landing square.
steps.prompt: Capture both black men.
steps.wrong: Land on e5 after the first capture, then take f4.
steps.done: Both gone in one flight.

lessons.title: Crowning in the middle of a capture
lessons.summary: In Russian Checkers a man that reaches the far row during a capture becomes a king at once and keeps capturing as a king.
lessons.wrap: Crowning doesn’t stop a capture in Russian Checkers. Next: the Turkish strike.

steps.text:
If a man reaches the far row in the middle of a capture, it is crowned at once. If it can capture again, it carries on in the same move, as a flying king.

(In American checkers the move would stop on the crowning square.)
Jump to the far row, then keep going as a king.
steps.prompt: Capture both black men.
steps.wrong: Jump c7 to land on d8. You’re a king now: fly along the diagonal over f6.
steps.done: Crowned and captured again, in one move.

lessons.title: The Turkish strike rule
lessons.summary: In Russian Checkers captured pieces stay on the board until the move ends: no piece is jumped twice, and jumped pieces block the way.
lessons.wrap: Captured pieces come off at the end of the move. Next: how to win.

steps.text:
During a capture, the pieces you jump stay on the board until the whole move is over. Then they all come off together.

That has two effects: you can’t jump the same piece twice, and a piece you’ve already jumped blocks your path like any other piece.
Your king takes c3 and lands on e5. From there it can take f4 or d6, but not both: after taking f4 and landing on g3, the way back to d6 runs through f4, which is still on the board.
steps.prompt: Capture two black men.
steps.done: Two captured. The Turkish strike saved the third one.

steps.text: Quick check.
steps.prompt: Halfway through a capture, can your king jump back over a piece it has already captured?
options: Yes, it’s already off the board
No: it stays on the board until the move ends
steps.explain: No. Captured pieces are removed only at the end of the move, so they can’t be jumped twice and they block the way. Players call combinations that use this the Turkish strike.

lessons.title: How to win at Russian Checkers
lessons.summary: You win at Russian Checkers by capturing all your opponent’s pieces or leaving them with no legal move. Learn both, and the draw rules.
lessons.wrap: You know every rule of Russian Checkers. Test yourself in the rules check.

steps.text:
You win when your opponent can’t move. Usually that’s because you’ve captured all their pieces.

It also counts if every piece they have left is blocked.
Black has one man left.
steps.prompt: Win the game.
steps.done: No black pieces left: you win!

steps.text: Black’s last man is on h8. Its only move is to g7, where your man stands, and your man on f6 stops it capturing. Keep it that way.
steps.prompt: Win by leaving Black with no move.
steps.wrong: That lets Black move or capture. Leave g7 and f6 where they are.
steps.done: Black can’t move, so you win.

steps.text: And if neither side can win?
steps.prompt: Which of these is a draw in Russian Checkers?
options: The same position three times, or 15 moves each with only kings moving and no captures
Any time one player has more kings
steps.explain: Both of those are draws (and players can always agree a draw too). BoardGameSite applies them automatically.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Five questions on every rule. Pass to unlock combinations.

lessons.title: Russian Checkers rules quiz
lessons.summary: Test your knowledge of the Russian Checkers rules: flying kings, backward captures, free choice of captures and crowning mid-capture.
lessons.wrap: Rules check passed. Now for the combinations that win games.

steps.text: Question 1.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this king can move to.
steps.wrong: Kings fly any distance along a diagonal.
steps.done: Correct: nine squares.

steps.text: Question 2.
steps.prompt: Make the capture.
steps.done: A backward capture.

steps.text: Question 3.
steps.prompt: You have two captures: one takes one piece, the other takes three. Must you take three?
options: Yes, the biggest capture is compulsory
steps.explain: No. In Russian Checkers you may choose any capture, as long as you finish it.

steps.text: Question 4.
steps.prompt: Capture both black men in one move.
steps.wrong: Jump to the far row, then keep going as a king.
steps.done: Crowned mid-capture, then captured again.

steps.text: Question 5.
steps.prompt: Win the game in one move.
steps.done: Your king flies over the last piece.

units.name: Combinations
units.blurb: Forcing captures, safe pieces and trapping kings.

lessons.title: The two-for-one shot in Russian Checkers
lessons.summary: Give up one piece to force a capture, then take two back. The simplest combination in Russian Checkers, with a puzzle to solve.
lessons.wrap: Before every move, look for a piece you can give away to set up a bigger capture.

steps.text:
Captures are compulsory, so you can force your opponent to take a piece and land exactly where you want.

Give one, take two: that’s a two-for-one shot.
Offer a piece that Black must take. Their capturing man then becomes a stepping stone.
steps.prompt: Set up the shot: offer a piece.
steps.wrong: Look for a move that puts your man next to a black man, with an empty square behind it.
steps.done: Gave one, took two.

lessons.title: Watch your back: don’t leave pieces hanging
lessons.summary: In Russian Checkers men capture backwards, so a piece can be taken from behind. Learn to check every move for loose pieces.
lessons.wrap: Before you move, check every black man next to the square you’re leaving or landing on, in all four directions.

steps.text:
In American checkers a man that has passed the enemy is safe from it. Not here: black men capture backwards too.

Before every move, check whether the square you land on, or the one you leave, gives Black a capture.
Only one of your moves keeps all your men safe.
steps.prompt: Make a safe move.
steps.wrong: Black can capture after that, possibly backwards. Check c3, f6 and h4.
steps.done: Safe. Every other move let Black capture.

lessons.title: Luring a flying king into a trap
lessons.summary: A flying king must capture too. Offer it a piece so it lands where you can take it. Learn the king trap with a puzzle.
lessons.wrap: Compulsory capture applies to kings as well. Lure them onto the square you choose.

steps.text:
A king is worth about three men, so winning one is worth a sacrifice.

Because captures are compulsory, you can offer the king a piece so that it has to land on a square where you capture it.
The black king sits on the main road. Put a man on that diagonal so the king has to capture it and land on b2, right in front of your man on a1.
steps.prompt: Set the trap.
steps.wrong: Move a man onto the long diagonal, so the king has to capture it and land next to your man on a1.
steps.done: One man for a king: a great trade.

units.name: Endgames
units.blurb: The race to the first king and the main road.

lessons.title: Racing for the first king
lessons.summary: In Russian Checkers the first flying king often wins the game. Learn to count the race and run the right man safely.
lessons.wrap: Count moves to the far row, and run where no black man can capture you, forwards or backwards.

steps.text:
With few pieces left, the first king usually decides the game, and in Russian Checkers a flying king is even stronger than in American checkers.

Count how many moves each man needs to reach the far row.
Your man on f4 is closest. The black man on d6 can capture anything that lands on e5.
steps.prompt: Run the closest man forward safely.
steps.wrong: That square can be captured, or it doesn’t help the race. Go around the black man.
steps.done: Safe, and on the way to the crown.

lessons.title: The main road: the most important diagonal
lessons.summary: The long a1–h8 diagonal, the main road, decides many Russian Checkers endgames. A lone king that holds it can draw against three.
lessons.wrap: Hold the main road when you’re behind; take it when you’re ahead.

steps.text:
The main road is the long diagonal from a1 to h8. It crosses the whole board, so a king on it watches eight squares.

Three kings against one usually win, but only if the lone king does not hold the main road. If it does, the game is normally a draw.
You have one king against three. Get onto the main road where no black king can capture you.
steps.prompt: Put your king on the main road.
steps.wrong: Find the move that lands on the a1–h8 diagonal.
steps.done: On the main road. Now Black will struggle to win.
